entries_new.pop: Accompong grew from 85 in 1740 to 159 in 1788
entries_new.laws: Treaty left internal crimes to Maroon captains, except capital cases
entries_new.challenge: British colonists in the First Maroon War
entries_new.mechanism: A guerrilla war forced a treaty giving land and internal authority in exchange for military service and returning runaways.
entries_new.name: Jamaican Maroon treaties of 1739 and 1740
entries_new.story:
People who had freed themselves from slavery in Jamaica held mountain towns against British colonists in the First Maroon War (about 1728 to 1740). Governor Edward Trelawny ended it by treaty. The 1739 articles with Captain Cudjoe gave about 1,500 acres to his people and their descendants, let his successors punish crimes among themselves except by death, and put two white men in residence with him.
In return the Maroons had to help suppress rebels, repel invaders, and return runaways for a reward. Wikipedia reports that the eastern Windward treaty of 1740 is still in force.

sources.t: Jamaica 1739 treaty, full transcript, Slavery and Freedom Laws, UNB

entries_new.founder: Cudjoe and Accompong, per town tradition
entries_new.laws: Elected chief; autonomy under the 1739 treaty
entries_new.mechanism: Kept its treaty with the colonial power through a rebellion by another Maroon town, then carried the status into an independent Jamaica.
entries_new.name: Accompong Town
entries_new.story:
Accompong is a Maroon village in the Cockpit Country hills of St Elizabeth, Jamaica. The 1739 treaty did not name it, and the Assembly granted it 1,000 acres in 1756 after a land dispute with planters. After its leaders died, white superintendents appointed by the governor controlled the Leeward towns, and the superintendent held de facto power during the 1795 war, when Accompong fought for the British.
It was the one Leeward town that kept formal autonomy afterwards. Wikipedia says Jamaica ratified that autonomy at independence in 1962. A chief is elected by vote, and about 600 people live there.

entries_new.stopped_by: Governor Alexander Lindsay and the Jamaican Assembly
entries_new.mechanism: Held treaty land until a war with the colony ended in surrender and removal overseas.
entries_new.name: Trelawny Town and the deportation of 1796
entries_new.story:
Trelawny Town, also called Cudjoe's Town, was the largest of the five Jamaican Maroon towns and the town named in the 1739 land grant. Tension with Governor Alexander Lindsay led to the Second Maroon War of 1795 to 1796. The governor promised leniency if the Maroons surrendered, then with the Assembly's backing deported just under 600 of them to Nova Scotia.
In 1800 about 600 left Nova Scotia for Freetown in Sierra Leone. In the 1840s about 200 returned to Jamaica and settled at Flagstaff, now Maroon Town.

entries_new.challenge: Spanish expeditions; rebellions subdued in 1696 and 1713 to 1717
entries_new.recognition: Spanish Crown, by decree of 1691 and agreement of 1713
entries_new.mechanism: Palisaded settlement that traded an end to taking in new runaways for a Spanish grant of freedom and land.
entries_new.name: San Basilio de Palenque
entries_new.story:
San Basilio de Palenque is a village in Bolivar, northern Colombia, descended from a settlement of runaways. In 1599 about 30 people escaped under Benkos Bioho, and they settled behind palisades, which gave the place its name. Sources put his hanging in 1619 or 1621.
A Spanish royal decree of 1691 offered freedom if the town stopped taking escapees, but runaways kept coming. A 1713 agreement signed by Bishop Antonio Maria Casiani granted its land on the same condition. In 1772 it was placed within the Mahates district. About 3,500 people live there and speak the Palenquero creole.

entries_new.pop: Estimated from about 2,000 to several thousand
entries_new.mechanism: Hiding on islands in a swamp too difficult to police, trading labour and goods with outsiders.
entries_new.anchor: Great Dismal Swamp, Virginia and North Carolina
entries_new.name: Great Dismal Swamp maroons
entries_new.story:
People escaping slavery lived on dry raised ground inside the Great Dismal Swamp, on the Virginia and North Carolina border, from about 1700 to the 1860s. Herbert Aptheker estimated about 2,000 in 1939; later studies say thousands, and the exact number is unknown. Archaeologist Dan Sayers began the main fieldwork in 2002.
A militia with dogs entered in 1823 and most people escaped. North Carolina passed a law aimed at them in 1847. How free they were is debated: nearby whites often left them alone if they paid in logs or shingles. United States Colored Troops entered during the Civil War and most left after it.

entries_new.challenge: Dutch colonial forces; later the Afobaka dam and state concessions
entries_new.recognition: Dutch colonial authorities in 1762; abrogated after independence
entries_new.mechanism: A long rainforest war ended in a treaty recognising land and trade rights.
entries_new.name: Saramaka treaty of 1762
entries_new.story:
The Saramaka are a Maroon people on the upper Suriname River, descended from people who fled Dutch plantations in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. After nearly 100 years of fighting they signed a treaty in 1762 that acknowledged their territorial rights and trading privileges, a century before general emancipation in Suriname.
They lived almost as a state within a state until the mid-20th century. In the 1960s a hydroelectric dam built to power an aluminium smelter flooded about half their territory and displaced 6,000 people. After Suriname's independence the old treaties were abrogated. About 90,000 Saramaka now live in Suriname and French Guiana.

entries_new.pop: Roughly 55,000 by the article's count; about 90,000 by Wikipedia's
entries_new.challenge: Logging and mining concessions granted by Suriname
entries_new.mechanism: A human rights court ordered collective title within the state, not separate sovereignty.
entries_new.name: Saramaka People v. Suriname
entries_new.story:
This is a 2007 ruling of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights on Maroon land. In the 1990s Suriname allowed logging and mining firms into Saramaka territory without consulting its authorities. The Court ruled that Suriname must grant collective title under customary law, consult or obtain consent for projects, and pay into a US$675,000 development fund.
The Court treated the Saramaka as a tribal people with rights like those of Indigenous peoples, and did not give them independence: the land stays inside Suriname. Cultural Survival reported in 2012 that none of the orders had been carried out.

sources.t: Cultural Survival: Saramaka People v Suriname, a human rights victory and its messy aftermath

entries_new.challenge: Dutch colonial government; Surinamese Interior War of 1986 to 1992
entries_new.mechanism: Treaty granting territorial autonomy and trade, with a militarised border post set at Stoelmanseiland in 1791.
entries_new.name: Ndyuka treaty of 1760
entries_new.story:
The Ndyuka are a Maroon people on the Tapanahoni River in southeastern Suriname. After a slave rebellion in 1757 on six wood plantations, runaways joined an existing group estimated at 2,000 people in six villages. On 10 October 1760 they signed a treaty with the Dutch colonial authorities recognising their territorial autonomy. It was the first of its kind in Suriname, and article 7 worked as a free-trade agreement.
The Tapanahoni was off-limits to white colonists and not explored until the early 20th century. Wikipedia says the treaty still defines Ndyuka rights in the gold-rich interior, and also says Suriname abrogated the old treaties after independence.

entries_new.challenge: Society of Suriname; Ndyuka allied with the colony from 1789
entries_new.mechanism: Guerrilla war and retreat across a colonial border, ending in citizenship of the neighbouring power.
entries_new.name: Aluku (Boni) Maroons
entries_new.story:
The Aluku are a Maroon people now mainly in southwest French Guiana. They wanted a treaty like that of the neighbouring Ndyuka, but the Society of Suriname went to war with them. Their leader Boni retreated to Fort Boekoe in a swamp, which fell on 20 September 1772 to an army of 300 freed slaves.
They moved to the Lawa River, were driven out of Suriname by 1791, and Boni was killed in 1793 by a Ndyuka chief. A treaty of 1836 made by a French navy chemist with no authority was disowned by both colonies. In 1860 the Ndyuka allowed them to settle at Abouna Sounga. They officially became French citizens on 25 May 1891.

entries_new.mechanism: Hiding in coastal marsh, armed through contacts with free people of color and enslaved people.
entries_new.anchor: Lake Borgne, St Bernard Parish, Louisiana
entries_new.name: Bas du Fleuve and the San Malo band
entries_new.story:
Bas du Fleuve was the headquarters of a group of runaways led by Jean Saint Malo (Juan San Malo in Spanish) in the swamps east of New Orleans, on Lake Borgne in Spanish Louisiana. The band controlled canals and back-country passages between Lake Pontchartrain and the Gulf, and got weapons from free people of color and plantation slaves.
In 1783 Col. Francisco Bouligny led an expedition that captured 60 people, including Saint Malo, as part of a campaign that took over a hundred runaways. He was hanged for murder on 19 June 1784 in front of St Louis Cathedral.

entries_new.mechanism: Hilltop stronghold in dense jungle with separate hidden quarters for families, and alliances with pirates.
entries_new.name: Bayano's palenque at Ronconcholon
entries_new.story:
Bayano, an enslaved African, led a revolt in Panama in 1552, on a ship or after landing depending on the account. Sources give his forces as 400 to 1,200 cimarrones, the Spanish word for runaways. They set up a defended settlement called Ronconcholon near the Chepo River, also called Rio Bayano, and fought for over five years. Women who learned other languages worked as translators with pirates and gathered intelligence.
Viceroy Canete offered terms recognising their freedom if they took no newcomers and returned runaways. The cimarrones later helped Francis Drake against Spain.

entries_new.laws: Right to self-rule as a free town
entries_new.mechanism: Raids on the main colonial road forced talks, which produced a chartered free town that had to return runaways.
entries_new.name: Yanga and San Lorenzo de los Negros
entries_new.story:
Around 1570 Gaspar Yanga and others escaped a sugar plantation and built a settlement in the highlands near Mt Orizaba, New Spain, which grew to about 500 people. They raided caravans on the road between Veracruz and Mexico City. A Spanish attack in 1609 under Pedro Gonzalo de Herrera produced no winner.
The outcome was a self-ruled free town, San Lorenzo de los Negros, recognised sometime between 1618 and 1641, on condition that it return further runaways. It was renamed Yanga in 1932 and lies in today's state of Veracruz.

entries_new.mechanism: A mine revolt followed by decades of being left alone, then formal recognition of freedom.
entries_new.name: Sierra del Cobre community
entries_new.story: In 1731 enslaved people rose up at the Cobre mines in eastern Cuba and set up an independent community in the Sierra del Cobre. It existed without serious interference for fifty years, and by 1781 its self-freed population had passed 1,000. That year the Spanish colonial authorities agreed to recognise the freedom of its people.

entries_new.mechanism: Mountain settlements that traded by boat with nearby islands.
entries_new.anchor: Sierra Maestra and Moa mountains, eastern Cuba
entries_new.name: Palenques of Bumba, Maluala and Moa
entries_new.story:
These were settlements of runaways in the mountains of eastern Cuba, where people joined Taino refugees. In the 1810s Ventura Sanchez led several hundred near Santiago de Cuba until he was tricked into the city and killed himself to avoid capture, and Manuel Grinan took over. Bumba sent small boats to trade with Jamaica and Santo Domingo.
Spanish expeditions went against Bumba and Maluala in 1830, and Antonio de Leon destroyed Bumba. Those at Moa and Maluala lasted until the war of 1868, when many joined the Cuban Liberation Army.

entries_new.pop: Thousands, per the Office of the Capture of Maroons
entries_new.mechanism: Small groups sheltering in caves on limestone hills.
entries_new.name: Palenques of western Cuba
entries_new.story: In the 1830s runaway settlements thrived in western Cuba, especially around San Diego de Nunez. The colonial Office of the Capture of Maroons reported thousands of runaways in these palenques between 1797 and 1846. Researchers have identified 28 archaeological sites linked to runaways in the Vinales Valley, mostly from the early 19th century, with people using caves for varying lengths of time.

entries_new.mechanism: Armed bands holding the interior of the island and joining the Taino chief Enriquillo in the Bahoruco Mountains.
entries_new.name: Maroons of Hispaniola
entries_new.story:
The earliest runaway communities in the Americas formed on Hispaniola. Governor Ovando complained of escapees in 1503, and a revolt on Diego Columbus's sugar plantations on 26 December 1522 was crushed, though many got away. Sebastian Lemba rebelled in 1532 and fought for 15 years until his capture in 1547 or 1548.
By the 1540s these groups controlled the island's interior. Archdeacon Alonso de Castro estimated 2,000 to 3,000 people in 1542. Roads were so unsafe that Spaniards travelled only in groups. Maroons were present across the island until the mid-17th century.

entries_new.mechanism: Retreat into mountain forest until the colony offered freedom in exchange for catching runaways.
entries_new.anchor: Bahoruco mountains, Haiti and Dominican Republic border
entries_new.name: Bahoruco Maroons and the 1785 terms
entries_new.story:
Runaways from French Saint-Domingue lived in the Bahoruco mountains from the late 17th century. French expeditions in 1702, 1719, 1728 and 1733 captured some but failed to end them, and a joint French and Spanish force in 1776 to 1777 found the villages empty and lost soldiers to illness and desertion.
In 1782 de Saint-Larry offered peace terms to the leader Santiago: freedom in return for hunting other runaways. Terms were agreed at the end of 1785, and the more than 100 people under Santiago stopped raiding.

entries_new.founder: Escaped enslaved people; leaders include Sans Souci and Barbe Blanche
entries_new.stopped_by: French militias under Mahe de La Bourdonnais
entries_new.mechanism: Hiding in the island's wild interior and attacking colonial posts.
entries_new.name: Maroons of Mauritius and Le Morne
entries_new.story:
In 1642, 50 of the first 105 enslaved people brought to Dutch Mauritius escaped, and only 18 were caught. On 18 June 1695 a group of Indonesian and Chinese origin set fire to the Dutch fort in an attempt to take the island, and all were caught and decapitated. They stayed behind when the Dutch left in 1710.
The French faced attacks from 1715. Mahe de La Bourdonnais raised militias after 1735. Leader Sans Souci was captured in 1739 and burnt alive. Barbe Blanche escaped pursuit at Le Morne, a peninsula whose legend says runaways leapt to their deaths in 1835 when police came to tell them slavery had ended.

entries_new.mechanism: Refuge in the mountainous interior of the island.
entries_new.name: Maroons of Reunion
entries_new.story: Reunion in the Indian Ocean had runaway groups whose leaders included Cimendef, Cotte, Dimitile and Maffate. In the 18th century Dimitile rebelled and found asylum in a part of the island that took his name. In 1743 he and his companions are said to have freed Jeanneton, a woman enslaved from Mozambique, from her owner Pierre Hibon. The first people in the Cilaos caldera were runaways, who were tracked and recaptured by armed slaveholders; official settlement there dates only from around 1850.

entries_new.mechanism: River island settlements close to plantation country.
entries_new.name: Abercorn Island maroons, Georgia
entries_new.story: In the late 18th century runaways set up two settlements on Abercorn Island, then called Belleisle, on the Savannah River upstream of Savannah in today's Effingham County, Georgia. A local militia destroyed them in 1787. The survivors built another settlement at Bear Creek, which was also raided, and its leader was killed.

entries_new.mechanism: Moving to a free territory and settling together alongside Native American neighbours.
entries_new.name: Lakeview, Illinois
entries_new.story: Lakeview in Illinois was founded as a Freedmen's town by a group of African American runaways and freed people who came from North Carolina shortly after the War of 1812, arriving between 1818 and 1820. The Maroons article reports that the community integrated with the Native Americans still living, hunting and farming in the area. It gives no separate government for the town.

entries_new.mechanism: Forest settlements allied with the Kalinago.
entries_new.name: Maroons of Dominica
entries_new.story: On Dominica in the Caribbean, people who escaped slavery joined the Indigenous Kalinago in the island's densely forested interior and created Maroon communities. These were in constant conflict with the British colonial authorities throughout the period of slavery. The Maroons article gives no treaty or end date beyond that period.

entries_new.stopped_by: British division under General John Moore
entries_new.mechanism: An alliance of runaways with French soldiers holding the island's interior against British occupation.
entries_new.name: Army in the Woods, Saint Lucia
entries_new.story:
After Britain captured Saint Lucia on 1 April 1794, runaways and fugitive French regulars formed the Armee Francaise dans les Bois (French Army in the Woods), about 6,000 men, who fought the First Brigand War. Under French Commissioner Gaspard Goyrand they retook most of the island.
On 26 May 1796 about 2,000 men at Morne Fortune surrendered to a British division under General John Moore. Over 2,500 prisoners were shipped to Portchester Castle in England and later exchanged. Anse Mamin is recorded as the colony's first maroon village.

entries_new.mechanism: A rebel capital in the mountains beside a silver route.
entries_new.name: Miguel's rebellion at San Pedro, Honduras
entries_new.story:
In 1548 in what is now Honduras, enslaved people at San Pedro rebelled under a self-freed man named Miguel, who set up his own capital. The area lay on trade routes that carried silver from the Pacific side to the coast at Trujillo and Puerto Caballos. Spain sent reinforcements to put the revolt down.
In 1648 Thomas Gage reported bands numbering in the hundreds along these same routes.

entries_new.mechanism: Shipwreck survivors merged into a coastal people and rose to lead it.
entries_new.name: Miskito Sambu
entries_new.story: The Miskito Sambu are a people of mixed African and Indigenous descent on the Mosquito Coast of Central America. Early accounts say enslaved people revolted on a ship and wrecked it near Cape Gracias a Dios, with dates given as 1639, 1641 or 1649. Exquemelin wrote that locals re-enslaved them, de Lussan that they were welcomed and married in, and Bishop Garret y Arlovi that they overthrew their hosts. The group rose to leadership on the coast, and in the first half of the 18th century led large slave raids into Spanish-held territory.

entries_new.mechanism: Palisaded settlement in river country.
entries_new.name: Palenque on the Magdalena River
entries_new.story: At the start of the 17th century a group of runaways set up a palisaded settlement on the outskirts of the Magdalena River in what is now Colombia. In 1654 Don Pedro Zapata, governor of Cartagena de Indias, defeated it. The same region had seen enslaved rebels destroy Santa Marta in 1529.

entries_new.challenge: Spanish peace offer of 1732, rejected; defeat in 1745
entries_new.mechanism: Refused the usual terms of freedom in exchange for returning runaways.
entries_new.name: Palenque of Castillo, Popayan
entries_new.story: Runaways established the Castillo settlement in the Popayan district of what is now Colombia. In 1732 Spanish authorities offered peace terms with a clause requiring the return of runaways, and Castillo's rulers rejected it. In 1745 colonial forces defeated the settlement, and over 200 African and Indian runaways surrendered.

entries_new.mechanism: River settlements beyond colonial reach.
entries_new.name: Free communities of Esmeraldas, Ecuador
entries_new.story: On Ecuador's northern coast, runaways and shipwreck survivors formed independent communities along the rivers, mixing with Indigenous peoples beyond the reach of the colonial government. The Maroons article lists separate groups in the cantons of Cojimies y Tababuela, Esmeraldas and Limones.

entries_new.pop: At least 300 in 1744; over 2,000 in the region by 1782
entries_new.mechanism: Forest camps beyond the plantation colonies.
entries_new.name: Maroon camps of Essequibo, Guyana
entries_new.story: In 1744 Dutch officials sent an expedition against camps of at least 300 runaways in the Northwest district of Essequibo, in modern Guyana, and nailed the severed hands of those they killed to posts as a warning. In 1782 a French official estimated more than 2,000 runaways around Berbice, Demerara and Essequibo.

entries_new.mechanism: A fortified settlement that traded cocoa and raided nearby towns.
entries_new.name: Cumbe of Ocoyta, Venezuela
entries_new.story: A cumbe is the Venezuelan word for a settlement of runaways. Guillermo Ribas ran away in 1768 and formed one at Ocoyta in the Barlovento region, with people of African and Indian origin who traded cocoa and reportedly attacked the towns of Chuspa and Panaquire. In 1771 German de Aguilera's expedition destroyed it and killed Guillermo, but captured only eight adults and two children. His deputy Ubaldo, born a slave in London, was caught in 1772.

entries_new.laws: Republic with democratic voting
entries_new.mechanism: A voting republic that federated with four neighbouring settlements.
entries_new.anchor: Itapocu, Brazil; pin at regional level only
entries_new.name: Mola quilombo and the Itapocu confederation
entries_new.story: A quilombo is a Brazilian settlement of people who escaped slavery. Mola held about 300 people, first led by Felipa Maria Aranha and later also by Maria Luiza Piria. It was organised as a republic with voting and in time expanded to include four similar settlements, known as the Confederacao do Itapocu. Traces of it could still be seen in 1895, and by 2020 they had disappeared.

entries_new.mechanism: Modern environmental designation over land occupied by descendants of runaways.
entries_new.name: Curiau, Amapa
entries_new.story: Curiau is a group of Black rural settlements near Macapa, the capital of the Brazilian state of Amapa, listed among surviving quilombos. In 1992 the Rio Curiau Environmental Protection Area was created for the people of Curiau de Dentro, Curiau de Fora, Casa Grande, Curralinho and Mocambo. It covers 21,676 hectares and in 1999 held about 1,500 people. The protection comes from a state designation and carries no separate government.

entries_new.stopped_by: Force led by Joaquim da Costa Cardozo
entries_new.mechanism: A small hidden settlement close to a colonial capital.
entries_new.name: Buraco de Tatu
entries_new.story: Buraco de Tatu was a small runaway settlement, or mocambo, in Bahia, Brazil, located between Salvador and Itapoa. It thrived for 20 years from 1743 to 1763 until a force led by Joaquim da Costa Cardozo destroyed it.

entries_new.mechanism: A dispersed network that dodged tax and regrouped after raids.
entries_new.name: Quilombo do Campo Grande
entries_new.story: Campo Grande in Minas Gerais, Brazil, developed through the 18th century as a scattered network of settlements tied by kinship and shared interests, in particular the refusal to pay the per capita tax. Farming, gathering, hunting and trade supported it, and people moved and reoccupied land when attacked. In 1741 Jean Ferreira led an expedition against it, in 1746 another captured 120 people, and in 1752 an expedition under Pere Marcos was attacked with heavy losses.

entries_new.stopped_by: Forces of Luis Pinto de Sousa Coutinho
entries_new.laws: Queen, parliament and counsellor
entries_new.mechanism: An armed settlement on a remote frontier that paid its way by selling cloth and food.
entries_new.name: Quilombo do Piolho (Quariterê)
entries_new.story:
This quilombo, a Brazilian settlement of people who escaped slavery, stood between the Guapore River and Cuiaba in Mato Grosso. It was headed by Jose Piolho and, after his death, by his widow Tereza de Benguela, who ran it with a parliament and a counsellor. It grew cotton, wove cloth for sale outside, and got guns by trade.
Forces of Luis Pinto de Sousa Coutinho destroyed it in 1770, and its 79 Black and 30 Indigenous people were killed or arrested. The Quilombo article lists a Carlota settlement in Mato Grosso from 1770 to 1795 separately.

aka: Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose
entries_new.founder: Governor Manuel de Montiano; Francisco Menendez
entries_new.mechanism: A colonial power gave runaways freedom and a town in return for conversion and defending its border against a rival empire.
entries_new.anchor: Fort Mose Historic State Park, St Augustine, Florida
entries_new.name: Fort Mose
entries_new.story:
Fort Mose was a settlement two miles north of St Augustine in Spanish Florida, the first free Black town legally sanctioned in what became the United States. A Spanish decree of 1693 gave runaways from the British colonies asylum if they became Catholic and served four years in the militia. Governor Manuel de Montiano set up the fort in 1738 under Francisco Menendez, a Mandinga man who had escaped Carolina.
About 100 people lived behind its wall. It was abandoned after the Battle of Bloody Mose in 1740, rebuilt nearby and occupied from 1752 to 1763.

entries_new.founder: British officers including Edward Nicolls and George Woodbine
entries_new.stopped_by: US forces under Col. Duncan Clinch, with Creek allies
entries_new.mechanism: Inherited a fully armed fort from a departing empire, on land Spain owned but did not control.
entries_new.name: Negro Fort at Prospect Bluff
entries_new.story:
British forces built this fort in 1814 on the Apalachicola River in Spanish Florida, during the War of 1812, with Black and Native American labour. After the British left, runaways who farmed for miles along the river held it, with cannon and thousands of muskets.
On orders passed from Andrew Jackson, US and allied Creek forces attacked inside Spanish territory. On 27 July 1816 a heated shot hit the magazine and the explosion destroyed it. Col. Duncan Clinch reported nearly 300 casualties. Wikipedia calls this the only time the US destroyed a community of escaped slaves in another country.

entries_new.challenge: US removal; later Seminole Nation membership rules
entries_new.mechanism: Alliance with a Native people in a territory Spain claimed but did not closely control.
entries_new.name: Black Seminole towns in Florida
entries_new.story:
Black Seminoles descend from Seminole people, free Africans and people who escaped slavery and allied with Seminole groups in Spanish Florida. They lived in distinct bands near the Seminole, some held as slaves by Seminole leaders but with more freedom than slaves of whites, including the use of firearms. Those removed to Indian Territory in the 1830s kept that identity.
In 2000 the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma voted to limit membership to descendants on the Dawes Rolls, excluding about 1,200 Freedmen. In 2022 a US district court ruled that the Freedmen kept membership and voting rights.

entries_new.mechanism: Crossing an international border and offering military service to the state on the other side.
entries_new.name: Mascogos of El Nacimiento
entries_new.story:
The Mascogos are a people in Coahuila, Mexico, descended from Black Seminoles. After removal from Florida to Indian Territory, a group led by Wild Cat and John Horse moved to northern Mexico and settled at El Nacimiento in 1852. They worked for the Mexican government to protect against Indian raids. In exchange they lived beyond the reach of US slavery.
Many Seminoles died of smallpox and many others returned to the US. In May 2017 Coahuila's governor signed a decree recognising the group as an Indigenous people of the state.

entries_new.mechanism: Runaways and shipwreck survivors merged with the Island Carib on land not yet held by plantations.
entries_new.name: Garifuna of Saint Vincent
entries_new.story:
The Garifuna are an Afro-Indigenous people who originated on Saint Vincent in the Caribbean. Their African ancestors' arrival is disputed: Governor William Young's 1795 report said shipwrecked Africans from 1635 lived independently, while modern researchers say most were runaways from Barbados, St Lucia and Grenada whom the Caribs sheltered. British use of the label Black Carib has been described as casting them as interlopers without land claims.
Britain deported them in 1797 to the coast of Honduras. The founding diaspora on Roatan is estimated at 2,500 to 5,000 people.

entries_new.mechanism: A faction split from a treaty people and got a treaty of its own.
entries_new.name: Matawai treaty of 1769
entries_new.story:
The Matawai are a Maroon people in Suriname who began as part of the Saramaka and shared their 1762 peace. After the death of captain Abini, captains Beku and Musinga split away, and in 1769 the Matawai signed a separate treaty with the Dutch colonists. They asked the government for weapons against the raiding Kwinti.
Their granman, the paramount chief, is based at Poesoegroenoe. Of 19 villages, six were abandoned in the Surinamese Interior War. In the 1970s almost half the population had moved towards the capital.

entries_new.mechanism: A late treaty that gave a limited, mapped area of control around two villages.
entries_new.name: Kwinti treaty of 1887
entries_new.story:
The Kwinti are a small Maroon people on the Coppename River in Suriname, with about 300 people in 2014. Their origin is told in two ways: the Berbice uprising of 1763 or a plantation in Para. They were attacked many times in the late 18th century by the Matawai and by colonists.
They signed the last of the Maroon treaties in 1887, more than a century after the others. It made Alamun a head captain, ranked below a granman, over those on the Coppename, while those on the Saramacca stayed under the Matawai. In 1894 their area was fixed around Bitagron and Kaaimanston because of nearby wood and balata concessions.

entries_new.mechanism: A constitutional land title for descendants of runaways, inside the state.
entries_new.name: Brazil's quilombo land right (Article 68)
entries_new.story:
Article 68 of the transitional provisions of Brazil's 1988 Constitution recognises the definitive ownership of land by remaining quilombo communities that occupy it, and says the state must issue titles. The first title went to Boa Vista in the Amazon in November 1995. By July 2023 the Comissao Pro-Indio counted 211 titled territories, 62 only partly, with 1,787 titling cases pending.
The 2022 census counted about 1.3 million quilombolas, of whom 167,202 lived in officially delimited territories. The right gives ownership of land, with Brazilian law and courts still applying.

sources.t: Politize: titling of quilombola lands in Brazil
Comissao Pro-Indio: Quilombola communities in Brazil

entries_new.mechanism: Settlers on a colonial frontier declared a republic against a company government.
entries_new.name: Republic of Swellendam
entries_new.story: In 1795 burghers (Dutch settler citizens) at Swellendam in the Cape, angry with the Dutch East India Company, revolted and on 17 June declared a republic, with Hermanus Steyn as President. They called themselves national burghers after the style of the French Revolution. About sixty citizens under Petrus Delport had forced out the magistrate, over company taxes and a ban on registering Khoikhoi children on farms. Wikipedia's article on the republic says there was no intention to set up a republic, and that the government was recognised in the Free Republic of the Netherlands. It ended on 4 November 1795, when Great Britain occupied the Cape.

entries_new.challenge: British invasion of the Cape; 1799 revolt put down
entries_new.mechanism: Frontier farmers rejected colonial policy and declared independence.
entries_new.name: Republic of Graaff-Reinet
entries_new.story: Frontier farmers and the Cape government could not agree on frontier policy, and in the Cape Frontier Rebellion of 1795 the Boers (Dutch-speaking settlers) declared Graaff-Reinet an independent republic. After Britain invaded the Cape in 1795 it took possession of the area. A further revolt in 1799 was suppressed by British troops the same year.

entries_new.challenge: Zulu Kingdom; British forces at Port Natal
entries_new.mechanism: Mass migration past the colonial frontier, a land grant from a local king, then war and a new ally on the throne.
entries_new.name: Natalia Republic
entries_new.story:
Natalia was a Boer republic founded in 1839 by Voortrekkers, settlers who had left the British Cape Colony, in what is now KwaZulu-Natal. Zulu King Dingane granted Piet Retief land, then killed him and his 70-man delegation. Voortrekkers won at Blood River on 16 December 1838 and allied with Dingane's brother Mpande.
Britain occupied Port Natal in order to stop a Boer republic getting a harbour giving access to the interior. In 1843 Britain annexed the republic as the Colony of Natal. Most Voortrekkers moved northwest to the lands that became the Orange Free State and the South African Republic.

entries_new.founder: Louis Tregardt and Jan van Rensburg
entries_new.mechanism: A group split from the main trek and settled far beyond any government.
entries_new.name: Zoutpansberg
entries_new.story: Boers came to Zoutpansberg in 1835 under Louis Tregardt and Jan van Rensburg, settling along the Limpopo River in the far north of what is now South Africa. They had a reputation for lawlessness. In 1864, after the Transvaal Civil War, the area was incorporated into the South African Republic, where as a district it had the largest native population in the republic.

entries_new.laws: Own constitution from 1858; own Volksraad parliament
entries_new.recognition: Britain, by the Sand River Convention
entries_new.mechanism: Won a treaty from the colonial power, then held recognised independence for fifty years until conquest.
entries_new.name: South African Republic (Transvaal)
entries_new.story:
The South African Republic, or Transvaal, was a Boer state north of the Vaal River. In the Sand River Convention of 1852 Britain agreed the Boers there could govern themselves under their own laws, on condition of no slavery. Citizenship was first limited to members of the Dutch Reformed Church, then widened to other Dutch Calvinist churches in 1858.
The Boers won the First Boer War and kept independence. British forces occupied it in the war of 1899, using scorched-earth policies and concentration camps against those who fought on. It became the Transvaal Colony in 1902.

sources.t: Sand River Convention, text, Reitz appendix

entries_new.recognition: Britain, by the Orange River Convention of 1854
entries_new.mechanism: Independence handed over by a colonial power that no longer wanted the cost of ruling.
entries_new.name: Orange Free State
entries_new.story:
The Orange Free State was a Boer republic between the Orange and Vaal rivers. Britain proclaimed the region the Orange River Sovereignty in 1848, then wanted to drop the cost of running it. At a public meeting in Bloemfontein in June 1852 the vast majority of Europeans voted to stay under British rule, but the British handed it over anyway under the Orange River Convention of 23 February 1854.
It was annexed in 1900 as the Orange River Colony and ended as a republic on 31 May 1902 under the Treaty of Vereeniging.

entries_new.currency: South African pound; own postage stamps
entries_new.laws: Nearly identical to the South African Republic's
entries_new.mechanism: Mercenaries paid in land declared the land a state, with the consent of local chiefs.
entries_new.name: Republic of Stellaland
entries_new.story:
Stellaland was a Boer republic west of the Transvaal in what is now North West Province, South Africa. Boer mercenaries in a chiefs' feud were paid with 416 farms of about 2,563 hectares each, and on 26 July 1882 they declared independence under Gerrit van Niekerk. It held an estimated 20,500 people, 3,000 of European ancestry.
It printed stamps and used the South African pound. Whether any country recognised it is unclear. Britain called its leaders freebooters and marauders. Cecil Rhodes feared its plan to tax trade on a main route, and Britain abolished it in 1885.

entries_new.mechanism: Settlers won a chief's approval for a state on land Britain was also claiming.
entries_new.name: State of Goshen
entries_new.story: Goshen, named after the biblical land, was founded in October 1882 by Nicolaas Claudius Gey van Pittius in the Rooigrond area beside Stellaland, in what is now South Africa, with the approval of chief Moshette. It covered 10,400 square kilometres and held an estimated 17,000 people, about 2,000 of European origin. In 1883 it merged with Stellaland to form the United States of Stellaland, which Britain abolished in 1885.

entries_new.recognition: Germany and the South African Republic
entries_new.mechanism: Traded military help in a succession dispute for land, then asked to join a larger Boer state.
entries_new.name: Nieuwe Republiek
entries_new.story:
The New Republic was a small Boer state in present-day South Africa, proclaimed on 16 August 1884 on 13,600 square kilometres given by treaty with the Zulu Kingdom. Around 150 Boers and some Germans had offered Dinizulu, heir to the Zulu throne, military help in exchange for land in April 1884. The Transvaal government disapproved, probably nominally, since so many of its officials took part.
Only Germany and the South African Republic recognised it. President Lucas Meyer requested incorporation into the South African Republic on 20 July 1888.

entries_new.founder: William Worthington Jordan; President George Prinsloo
entries_new.cost: 300 pounds, in guns, a horse and brandy
entries_new.mechanism: A private purchase from a local chief, given to migrating settlers as the basis of a state.
entries_new.name: Upingtonia (Lijdensrust)
entries_new.story:
Upingtonia was a Boer republic in what is now Namibia, declared on 20 October 1885 with about 500 settlers. William Worthington Jordan bought some 50,000 square kilometres from Ondonga chief Kambonde for 300 pounds, paid as 25 firearms, a salted horse and a cask of brandy, and gave land free to returning Dorsland trekkers at Grootfontein.
The name honoured Cape prime minister Thomas Upington, who gave little support, and it became Lijdensrust in 1886. The state fought the Herero and came to depend on German protection. Jordan was killed in 1886, and it merged into German South-West Africa in 1887.

entries_new.founder: Joachim Ferreira, Frans Maritz; President Johannes Bezuidenhoudt
entries_new.laws: Own constitution and laws from 1886
entries_new.mechanism: A grazing concession was treated as ownership, subdivided and turned into a state.
entries_new.name: Klein Vrystaat
entries_new.story:
Klein Vrystaat, Afrikaans for Little Free State, was a tiny Boer republic near today's Piet Retief, South Africa. In 1877 Swazi king Mbandzeni granted 36,000 acres to two hunters, Ferreira and Maritz, on what he believed was a permanent grazing concession. They subdivided it into small farms.
Mbandzeni later let them form a council. In 1886 they adopted a constitution, with a president, Johannes Bezuidenhoudt, and laws. The South African Republic incorporated it in 1891.

entries_new.founder: Delegates from 28 towns; Green Mountain Boys under Ethan Allen
entries_new.challenge: New York's land claims; Continental Congress refused recognition
entries_new.mechanism: Settlers with disputed land titles declared independence and bargained with two larger powers until one admitted them.
entries_new.name: Vermont Republic
entries_new.story:
Vermont was an unrecognised independent state in New England from 1777 to 1791. Delegates from 28 towns declared independence in January 1777 from Quebec, New Hampshire and New York, after overlapping land grants led to conflict. It issued its own copper coin, and its constitution forbade adult slavery with allowances for younger people.
The Continental Congress refused to recognise it because of New York's objections. Vermont negotiated to join British Quebec, then dropped that after Yorktown. It was admitted to the US on 4 March 1791, with its constitution and laws continuing in effect.

entries_new.currency: Barter in goods, with foreign and federal coin accepted
entries_new.laws: Holston Constitution, modelled on North Carolina's
entries_new.mechanism: Settlers left behind by a failed land cession set up a state and asked to be admitted.
entries_new.name: State of Franklin
entries_new.story:
Franklin was an unrecognised state in present-day East Tennessee, created in 1784 after North Carolina offered the land to Congress and then took the offer back. It sought to become the 14th US state and failed.
It ran courts, created counties and adopted the Holston Constitution. Debts could be paid in corn, tobacco, apple brandy or skins, and governor John Sevier was often paid in deer hides. It made its own treaties with the Cherokee. After 1787 it ran alongside a re-established North Carolina government, and North Carolina took back full control after about four and a half years.

entries_new.laws: Articles of the Watauga Association; no copy found
entries_new.mechanism: Settlers beyond the colonial line wrote their own compact for local government.
entries_new.name: Watauga Association
entries_new.story:
The Watauga Association was a semi-autonomous government formed in 1772 by frontier settlers on the Watauga River, at today's Elizabethton, Tennessee. Virginia's governor Lord Dunmore called it a dangerous example in 1774. Theodore Roosevelt later described its people as the first American-born men to set up a free and independent community.
No copy of its Articles survives, and related documents imply the settlers still saw themselves as British subjects. North Carolina annexed the area in November 1776, and it became Washington County in 1777.

entries_new.laws: Constitution based on Iowa's
entries_new.challenge: US government did not recognise it
entries_new.mechanism: A religious migration past the US border drafted its own state constitution and asked to be admitted.
entries_new.name: Provisional government of Deseret, 1849
entries_new.story:
Deseret was a proposed US state promoted by leaders of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, who had settled the Salt Lake Valley in 1847, then part of Mexico. Brigham Young and church elders adopted a constitution in March 1849. It covered most of the land the US had just taken from Mexico, including today's Utah and Nevada and the coast around Los Angeles and San Diego.
A provisional government with a legislature, governor and supreme court ran for nearly two years in 1849 and 1850. The US never recognised it.

entries_new.founder: 33 American immigrants; encouraged by John C. Fremont
entries_new.mechanism: Armed immigrants seized a town during a war that the neighbouring power was about to win.
entries_new.name: California Republic (Bear Flag Revolt)
entries_new.story:
In June 1846, 33 American immigrants in Mexican Alta California, who had entered without permission and were barred from buying or renting land, rebelled at Sonoma. Brevet Captain John C. Fremont of the US Army covertly encouraged them. The name California Republic appeared only on their flag.
They elected officers and set up no civil government. Their force of 100 to 200 men was folded into Fremont's California Battalion on 5 July. On 9 July 1846 US Navy Lieutenant Joseph Revere raised the US flag at Sonoma. It lasted from June 14 to July 9.

entries_new.founder: Sanford B. Dole, Lorrin A. Thurston
entries_new.stopped_by: Annexed at its own request by the United States
entries_new.challenge: Deposed Kingdom; President Cleveland refused annexation
entries_new.mechanism: A settler-descended elite overthrew a monarchy and kept a state running until the US would annex it.
entries_new.name: Republic of Hawaii
entries_new.story:
The Republic of Hawaii was a one-party state from July 4, 1894 until US annexation on August 12, 1898. In 1893 the Committee of Public Safety overthrew Queen Liliuokalani. President Grover Cleveland refused annexation, so the group wrote a new constitution while waiting.
Its leaders, Sanford Dole and Lorrin Thurston, were Hawaii-born descendants of American settlers. The US Blount Report identified US complicity in the overthrow: American officials immediately recognised the new government, and Marines were sent.

entries_new.mechanism: A private colonisation society bought coastal land and shipped freed people there, running it as its own colony.
entries_new.name: Mississippi-in-Africa
entries_new.story:
Mississippi-in-Africa was a colony in what is now Sinoe County, Liberia, founded by the Mississippi Colonization Society, which planters and slaveholders set up in June 1831 to remove free Black people from their state. The first settlers came in 1837 and built Greenville. Governor Josiah Finley was murdered by local fishermen in 1838.
In the late 1840s some 300 people freed under Isaac Ross's will were the largest group of emigrants. Liberia annexed the colony in 1842 by this article's date. Settlers and their descendants became the Americo-Liberian elite, who took power over the Indigenous people.

entries_new.founder: Maryland State Colonization Society; governor John Brown Russwurm
entries_new.stopped_by: Annexed by Liberia after Grebo and Kru attacks
entries_new.laws: Constitution and laws of 1847, based on the US Constitution
entries_new.cost: US$10,000 a year for 26 years from the Maryland legislature
entries_new.mechanism: A colonisation society with a trade monopoly turned into a state and then a small republic.
entries_new.name: Republic of Maryland (Maryland in Liberia)
entries_new.story:
This was a West African country on the coast around Harper, first settled in 1834 under the Maryland State Colonization Society, with a US$10,000-a-year state appropriation. It stayed out of the 1838 Commonwealth of Liberia because the society wanted its trade monopoly. It became a state in 1841, published a constitution in 1847 and declared independence on May 29, 1854.
The population was 900 to 1,000 in 1851. Grebo and Kru attacks followed. Unable to defend itself, it appealed to Liberia, and after a referendum Liberia annexed it in 1857.

entries_new.stopped_by: Internal split; dissolved by Paraguay's government
entries_new.cost: At least 60 pounds per man, with all assets
entries_new.mechanism: A cooperative shipped members to land granted by a foreign government eager for immigrants, and ran the colony by its own rules.
entries_new.name: New Australia, Paraguay
entries_new.story:
New Australia was a socialist settlement founded on 28 September 1893 by the labour organiser William Lane with 238 people. Its rules were a common-hold, teetotalism, life marriage and a brotherhood of English-speaking whites that preserved the colour line. Men paid at least 60 pounds and all assets. Paraguay's government, keen on settlers, offered a large area of good land.
Conflict over alcohol, relations with locals and Lane's leadership split it. Paraguay eventually dissolved the cooperative and gave each settler a plot. About 2,000 descendants still live in Paraguay.

entries_new.mechanism: A breakaway from a breakaway: the founder left his own colony to start stricter rules elsewhere in the same country.
entries_new.anchor: 72 km south of New Australia, Paraguay
entries_new.name: Colonia Cosme, Paraguay
entries_new.story: Cosme was a colony in Paraguay founded after a split in New Australia. In May 1894 William Lane and 58 others left over disputes about alcohol and his leadership and set up a new settlement 72 kilometres further south. The source does not give a date for its end. Some colonists founded other communes in Paraguay, while others went home to Australia or on to England.

entries_new.stopped_by: Failure of the colony; founder's death
entries_new.pop: Five, later fourteen families at founding
entries_new.mechanism: Bought land titles from a Paraguayan politician for an exclusive settlement, without any claim to leave Paraguayan law.
entries_new.name: Nueva Germania
entries_new.story:
Nueva Germania is a district of San Pedro Department in Paraguay, founded as a German settlement in 1886 or 1887 by Bernhard Forster and Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche, sister of the philosopher. Forster intended it as a racially exclusive model community built on antisemitic and eugenic ideas, and negotiated land titles with General Bernardino Caballero. Five, later fourteen, impoverished families from Saxony came.
Harsh conditions and short supplies undermined it, and Forster killed himself in 1889. The residents took over the town and distanced themselves from the founders' ideas. It now grows yerba mate and soy.

aka: Free Lands of the Lower Zaporozhian Host
entries_new.challenge: Poland-Lithuania, Crimean Khanate, Ottoman Empire, Russia
entries_new.mechanism: Armed settlers in empty borderland between empires, useful to each as a defence and playing them against each other.
entries_new.name: Zaporozhian Sich
entries_new.story:
The Zaporozhian Sich was a self-governing Cossack polity on the lower Dnieper River in today's Ukraine, in a region then called the Wild Fields. It began as Slavic colonists' defence against Crimean Tatar raids, with fortified camps below the river's rapids, and grew with refugees from devastated lands. Poland-Lithuania, the Crimean Khanate, Muscovy and Russia each claimed it at different times.
From 1657 to 1687 it was practically independent, with its own administration and 12,000 to 20,000 Cossacks. In 1775 Catherine the Great disbanded it and absorbed its land into Novorossiya. Some formed a Danubian Sich outside Russia until 1828.

entries_new.stopped_by: Russian Empire, then the end of the Host in 1918
entries_new.mechanism: Runaways settled a steppe no state ran, then traded military service for tax freedom and partial self-rule.
entries_new.name: Free territories of the Don Cossacks
entries_new.story:
The Don Cossack Host was an independent or autonomous polity on the middle and lower Don in southern Russia, from the end of the 16th century until 1918. Until then, Don Cossacks held free territories in the Wild Field, populated in part by runaway serfs and people who did not recognise landowners' power. Their name meant free people.
Under Moscow they kept tax exemption in exchange for guarding the south, and the tsar's authority was less absolute there. Stenka Razin, Kondraty Bulavin and Emelian Pugachev came from them. Since 1992 a Russian decree lets Cossacks enrol on a special register.

entries_new.founder: Antonio de Sousa Neto; Bento Goncalves
entries_new.laws: Constitution of 1843
entries_new.mechanism: Rich ranchers raised militias against imperial tariffs and declared a republic.
entries_new.name: Riograndense Republic
entries_new.story:
The Riograndense Republic, or Piratini Republic, was a de facto state in today's Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, proclaimed on 11 September 1836 by General Antonio de Sousa Neto during the Ragamuffin War. Ranchers rebelled because tariffs made imported beef cheaper than their jerky and leather. It had five capitals and a constitution signed in 1843.
Only the United Kingdom, France and Uruguay recognised it. The Ponche Verde Treaty of 1 March 1845 ended the war, with amnesty for rebels and freedom for enslaved men who fought for the republic.

entries_new.mechanism: A confederation with a neighbouring breakaway state.
entries_new.name: Juliana Republic
entries_new.story: The Juliana Republic was a short-lived breakaway in southern Brazil that declared independence in 1839 during the Ragamuffin War and formed a confederation with the Riograndense Republic. In November 1839 the war ended in its defeat and disappearance.

entries_new.recognition: Holy Roman Emperor and the Pope
entries_new.mechanism: A military order won imperial and papal charters to land it then conquered and governed as its own.
entries_new.name: State of the Teutonic Order
entries_new.story:
This was a state run by a monastic order of knights on the southeast Baltic coast. The Golden Bull of Rimini of 1226 and a papal bull of 1234 brought Prussia into the order's possession, and it conquered the Baltic Prussians from 1230. In 1346 it bought the Duchy of Estonia from Denmark for 19,000 Cologne marks.
It declined after Grunwald in 1410 and held Prussia as a fief of Poland after the Peace of Thorn in 1466. In 1525 the Prussian branch became the secular Duchy of Prussia. The Livonian branch lasted until 1561.

sources.t: State of the Teutonic Order, Wikipedia

aka: Order of Saint John on Rhodes
entries_new.mechanism: An armed religious order with papal backing seized an island from a weakened empire and ruled it directly.
entries_new.name: Knights Hospitaller on Rhodes
entries_new.story:
The Knights Hospitaller, a Catholic military order, had no temporal power in Cyprus after the fall of Acre in 1291 and planned to get their own land. They chose Byzantine Rhodes, with the Pope's approval. The emperor refused their offer of homage and sent troops. The city surrendered on 15 August 1310 after four years.
They ruled Rhodes as a sovereign territory for 212 years and withstood invasions in 1444 and 1480. In 1522 Sultan Suleiman landed 100,000 men, 200,000 in other sources, against about 7,000. After six months the survivors withdrew to Sicily.

entries_new.founder: Jan Matthys, John of Leiden, Bernhard Knipperdolling
entries_new.laws: Compulsory polygamy under John of Leiden; shared goods
entries_new.mechanism: Won a city's elections, then turned it into a closed religious kingdom.
entries_new.name: Munster Anabaptist kingdom
entries_new.story:
Radical Anabaptists, Christians who practised adult baptism, ruled the German city of Munster from February 1534, when they seized the city hall and made Bernhard Knipperdolling mayor, until June 1535. Pamphlets called the poor to come and share the town's wealth. John of Leiden, a tailor aged 25, proclaimed himself successor of David and made polygamy compulsory.
The Bishop's army besieged the starving city, and it fell on June 24, 1535. About 3,000 people died, by one contemporary source. The leaders were tortured and executed in January 1536, and the cages holding their bodies still hang on St Lambert's Church.

entries_new.stopped_by: Qing dynasty, with French and British aid
entries_new.mechanism: A mass religious movement and army that took a former imperial city as its capital.
entries_new.name: Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
entries_new.story:
The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom was a theocratic monarchy from 1851 to 1864 led by Hong Xiuquan, a Hakka man who called himself the younger brother of Jesus. It fought to overthrow China's Qing dynasty and at its height held areas of southern China with nearly 30 million people. In 1853 it took Nanjing and renamed it Tianjing, the heavenly capital.
A march on Beijing failed. Qing armies under Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang, eventually helped by French and British forces, retook most areas by early 1864, and Nanjing was under attack that June as Hong declared God would defend it.

entries_new.founder: Civic councils; Guillaume Farel, John Calvin
entries_new.laws: Ecclesiastical Ordinances; Consistory
entries_new.recognition: Savoy, by the Treaty of Saint-Julien, 1603
entries_new.mechanism: A city threw out its bishop, adopted a religious reform as law, and held out through alliances with stronger neighbours.
entries_new.name: Republic of Geneva
entries_new.story:
Geneva was an independent city-state from 1534, when it broke with its prince-bishop and the House of Savoy, and became a center of Calvinism under John Calvin. A church court, the Consistory, enforced morals; theologian Michael Servetus was burned for heresy in 1553. Alliances with Swiss cities, including Zurich in 1584, helped it stay independent.
Savoy's last attack, the Escalade of 1602, was repulsed, and the Treaty of Saint-Julien of 1603 recognised its independence. Revolutionary France annexed it in 1798. It was restored in 1813 and became a Swiss canton in 1815.

entries_new.laws: City charter of 1840; municipal court used habeas corpus
entries_new.challenge: Illinois neighbours, Missouri extradition, mob violence
entries_new.mechanism: Used a state charter's powers over a militia and a court to shield a religious community from outside law.
entries_new.name: Nauvoo and its charter
entries_new.story:
Joseph Smith moved Latter Day Saints from Missouri to Commerce, Illinois in 1839 and renamed it Nauvoo. Seeking their votes, both Illinois parties passed a broad city charter in 1840 giving it a militia and courts. The Nauvoo Legion reached at least 2,500 troops, against about 8,500 in the entire US Army in 1845.
City courts freed Smith on habeas corpus when others tried to extradite him. In 1844 he ordered the Legion to destroy the Nauvoo Expositor newspaper, was charged with inciting a riot and was killed by a mob in Carthage Jail. The militia lost its sanction in 1845, and the Saints were expelled by 1846.

entries_new.mechanism: Poor followers of a preacher built a town beyond state attention, and rejected the taxes and authority of the new republic.
entries_new.name: Canudos (Belo Monte)
entries_new.story:
Canudos, named Belo Monte by its people, was a settlement in the dry backlands of Bahia, Brazil, founded in 1893 by the itinerant preacher Antonio Conselheiro. Taxes rose under the new republic, and press and authorities branded the settlers monarchists. The town reportedly passed 30,000 people.
Three government expeditions failed. The fourth, under General Arthur Oscar, bombarded and razed it in October 1897, with about 150 survivors reported. Death estimates differ: Euclides da Cunha gave about 30,000, Robert Levine around 15,000, Joel Singer 5,000.

entries_new.laws: Articles of association: common goods, no pay
entries_new.cost: Land purchase in Butler County, Pennsylvania
entries_new.mechanism: A religious commune held everything under a contract inside US law, with no claim to government.
entries_new.name: Harmony Society
entries_new.story:
The Harmony Society was a German Christian sect that left Wurttemberg because of religious persecution. On February 15, 1805, about 400 people led by Johann Georg Rapp organised at Harmony, Pennsylvania, placing all their goods in common under articles that gave the group legal status in US law. They built three towns, in Pennsylvania and Indiana, the last at Economy.
Its wealth was probably US$2 million by 1868. By 1890 it was in debt with an aged membership, and it was dissolved in 1905 with a net worth of US$1.2 million.

entries_new.mechanism: Colonised a remote island and used elected county offices and a religious crown together.
entries_new.name: Beaver Island kingdom
entries_new.story:
James Strang, who claimed to succeed Joseph Smith as Latter Day Saint leader, moved his church to Beaver Island in Lake Michigan in 1848. About 300 people watched his crowning on July 8, 1850, with a crown of tin. About 12,000 people accepted his claims overall. Wikipedia says he never claimed to be king of the island or any place, only of his church.
Strangites came to monopolise local government, and tensions with fishermen rose. He served in the Michigan House from 1853. On June 16, 1856, two men shot him at St James harbour and took refuge on the USS Michigan. He died on July 9.

entries_new.founder: Albert, bishop of Riga, and crusaders
entries_new.mechanism: A church-run land held by bishops and military orders, directly under the Pope in law.
entries_new.name: Terra Mariana
entries_new.story: Terra Mariana, Latin for Land of Mary, was medieval Livonia, covering today's Estonia and Latvia, formed after the Livonian Crusade. It began on 2 February 1207 as a principality of the Holy Roman Empire, and in 1215 Pope Innocent III declared it directly subject to the Holy See. A papal legate divided it among bishoprics, Denmark's Duchy of Estonia and a military order. Church, order, nobles and towns struggled for supremacy throughout. It ended in 1561 during the Livonian War, split between Sweden, Lithuania and Denmark.

entries_new.stopped_by: Samogitians and Semigallians at Saule; papal order
entries_new.mechanism: Warrior monks given a share of land they conquered, with papal sanction.
entries_new.name: Livonian Brothers of the Sword
entries_new.story: The Sword Brethren were a Catholic military order of German knights set up in 1202 in Livonia by Albert, bishop of Riga, and sanctioned by Pope Innocent III in 1204. They fought Baltic and Finnic pagans in today's Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, and held land under military administration from their castles. Knights had to be noble and vow obedience, poverty and celibacy. A general assembly chose the grand master, who served for life. After defeat at the Battle of Saule in 1236, the Pope disbanded them in 1237, and those who stayed joined the Teutonic Order.

sources.t: Livonian Brothers of the Sword, Wikipedia

entries_new.mechanism: A scattered chain of mountain fortresses, each able to feed itself, held by a closely disciplined sect.
entries_new.name: Nizari Ismaili state (Alamut)
entries_new.story:
The Alamut state was founded by Hassan Sabbah after he took Alamut Castle in Persia in 1090. It was a network of fortresses across Persia and the Levant held by a minority Shia sect, surrounded by hostile territory, and it issued coins. Heavily outnumbered, it relied on self-sufficient forts, assassinations of leaders and psychological warfare; outsiders called its people Assassins.
Almost two centuries later its leadership capitulated to the invading Mongols in 1256, who later massacred many Nizaris. Most of what is known comes from hostile sources.

entries_new.laws: Twelve revolutionary articles; common property
entries_new.mechanism: Armed religious radicals seized land and built a new town with common property, funded by gold mines.
entries_new.name: Taborites and the town of Tabor
entries_new.story:
The Taborites were a radical faction of the Hussite religious movement in Bohemia. In spring 1420 a group led by Petr Hromadka seized Sezimovo Usti and nearby Hradiste Castle, and began building the model town of Tabor. They announced that there would be no servants or masters, that property would be held in common, and that there would be no taxation. They elected four military commanders, among them Jan Zizka.
Tabor's control of local gold mines supported it. A siege in June 1420 failed, and Zizka stopped the first anti-Hussite crusade at Vitkov Hill on 14 July.

entries_new.mechanism: Evicted people gathered around a religious leader and declared independent rule on land several governments disputed.
entries_new.name: Contestado holy communities
entries_new.story: The Contestado War of October 1912 to August 1916 was fought in inland southern Brazil, on land claimed by Parana, Santa Catarina and Argentina. A railway concession gave Brazil Railway Company 15 km of land each side of the track, and farmers were expelled. Thousands of laid-off railway workers and evicted peasants gathered around Jose Maria, a healer revered as a holy monk, who preached monarchy and effectively declared his community under an independent government. Landowners, backed by state police and the army, fought them.

entries_new.laws: Lease covenants banning listed trades
entries_new.cost: 6,500 acres; lace works with US$1 million capital
entries_new.mechanism: One man owned all land and controlled residents by lease, inside ordinary US law.
entries_new.name: Zion, Illinois under John Alexander Dowie
entries_new.story:
Zion is a city in Lake County, Illinois, founded by the faith healer John Alexander Dowie, who bought 6,500 acres in 1899 for his Christian Catholic Church. Dowie personally owned all the land and leased it for 1,100 years, reasoning that Jesus would return in 2000 and rule for 1,000 years. Bans covered gambling halls, hospitals, saloons, tobacco shops and other churches.
His Theocratic Party, formed in 1902, won every office unopposed. Creditors sued in 1903, reaching US$70,000 in claims. The court appointed receivers, then dissolved the receivership, and dismissed the bankruptcy petition in 1905. The population was 24,655 in 2020.

entries_new.mechanism: Bought land and ran a closed economy, with no claim to separate law.
entries_new.name: Amana Colonies
entries_new.story: The Amana Colonies are seven villages on 26,000 acres in Iowa, built by German Radical Pietists who were persecuted at home and called themselves the True Inspiration Congregations. They settled near Buffalo, New York, and moved to Iowa in 1856 for more isolation. For eighty years they kept a nearly self-sufficient economy, importing very little. They lived communally until 1932, when during the Depression members voted to form a for-profit company, the Amana Society. They now rely on tourism.

entries_new.stopped_by: Mass deaths following a US congressional visit
entries_new.mechanism: A foreign religious group leased remote land from a government by offering a strategic presence on a disputed border.
entries_new.name: Jonestown
entries_new.story:
Jonestown, formally the Peoples Temple Agricultural Project, was a remote commune in Guyana set up by Jim Jones's American religious group. In 1974 it negotiated a lease of over 3,800 acres near the disputed border with Venezuela, pitching an American presence there to a government fearing incursion. Jones thought Guyana small and poor enough to give him influence and protection.
On November 18, 1978, 918 people died in a coordinated mass murder-suicide, 909 of them in Jonestown, following the murder of five people including US Congressman Leo Ryan. A third were minors, and guards were ordered to shoot those fleeing.

entries_new.mechanism: A communal religious corporation inside Ohio law.
entries_new.name: Society of Separatists of Zoar
entries_new.story: Zoar in Ohio was founded in 1817 by German Radical Pietists fleeing religious oppression in Wurttemberg. All property was held in common, and elected trustees ran the farms, shops and factories. At its height in the 1850s the society owned over 10,000 acres and was worth about US$1 million. It lasted until 1898. The village now has 172 residents, and ten restored buildings are kept as a historic site.

entries_new.mechanism: An emigrant sect holding property in common, without claiming to leave US law.
entries_new.name: Bishop Hill Colony
entries_new.story: Bishop Hill in Illinois was a religious commune founded in 1846 by Swedish preacher Eric Jansson, who preached against the Lutheran Church and was forced out of Sweden during growing persecution. He said it would be a New Jerusalem. About 1,400 colonists left Sweden, and many of the first thousand died of disease on the way or stayed in New York. They began in dugouts, and by 1849 had a flour mill, two sawmills and a church. The commune was dissolved in 1861.

entries_new.stopped_by: Sultan of Muscat with British forces
entries_new.recognition: Treaty of Seeb with the Sultanate, 1920
entries_new.mechanism: An elected religious ruler held the mountain interior while the coast went another way, until oil made the interior valuable.
entries_new.name: Imamate of Oman
entries_new.story:
The Imamate of Oman was a series of states in interior Oman in which Ibadi Muslims elected an imam as ruler, from about 750 CE, with capitals at Rustaq and Nizwa. After 1783 the coast followed hereditary sultans in Muscat and the interior kept the elected imam. A rebellion from 1913 ended with the Treaty of Seeb in 1920, which left a de facto split.
The Iraq Petroleum Company's concession from the Sultan in 1937 raised the stakes for the interior. In the Jebel Akhdar War, which lasted until 1959, the Sultan with direct British support defeated Imam Ghalib Alhinai.

entries_new.laws: Sharia, in competition with customary law
entries_new.mechanism: Religious law used as a single authority over mountain peoples at war with an empire.
entries_new.name: Caucasian Imamate
entries_new.story: The Caucasian Imamate was a state founded by Muslim imams across Dagestan and Chechnya during the Caucasian War of 1817 to 1864, in resistance to Russian expansion. It tried to unite many peoples under sharia law, which local rulers and communities that followed customary law resisted. Imam Shamil led from 1834 for 25 years, turning it into a centralised state. He sought British support, but no alliance came. Losses, including the Siege of Akhoulgo in 1839, weakened it, and it dissolved after his capture in 1859.

entries_new.founder: Muhammad bin Saud and Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab
entries_new.mechanism: A pact between a preacher and a local ruler combined religious authority with an expanding army.
entries_new.name: Emirate of Diriyah (first Saudi state)
entries_new.story:
The Emirate of Diriyah existed in Arabia from 1744 to 1818. It began with a pact between Muhammad bin Saud, emir of the Najdi town of Diriyah, and religious leader Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, joining a reform doctrine with political rule. It conquered Najd, the eastern coast and, from 1803, the Hejaz. Its forces captured Karbala in 1801 and, according to Wikipedia, killed over 5,000 civilians.
Egyptian forces under Ottoman orders besieged and destroyed Diriyah in 1818.

entries_new.laws: Right to administer justice
entries_new.mechanism: A host king gave a military order frontier land, then expelled it when it sought independence from him.
entries_new.name: Teutonic Knights in Burzenland
entries_new.story: In 1211 King Andrew II of Hungary gave the Burzenland, now Tara Barsei in Transylvania, Romania, to the Teutonic Knights to guard his border against the Cumans. He kept coinage and mineral claims, and gave them the right to hold markets and administer justice, free of taxes. They built five castles. In 1225 he expelled them after they tried to set up an autonomous monastic principality answerable only to the Pope. They moved on to Prussia.

entries_new.founder: Emperor Charles V; Order of St John
entries_new.mechanism: A religious order that had lost its land received a new island as a fief from a friendly emperor.
entries_new.name: Hospitaller Malta
entries_new.story:
Hospitaller Malta was a de facto state from 1530 to 1798 in which the Order of St John ruled Malta and Gozo. Formally a vassal of Sicily, it arose when Emperor Charles V granted the islands and Tripoli to the Order after it lost Rhodes. It lost Tripoli in 1551, survived an Ottoman siege in 1565 and built Valletta.
The Order weakened after the French Revolution. Napoleon's forces invaded and expelled it in 1798. The Treaty of Amiens of 1802 said Malta would go back, but Britain stayed, and the Treaty of Paris of 1814 made it a British colony.

zones_new.name: Runaway communities (maroons)
zones_new.who_owns: Every historic site now lies inside a recognised country. Some descendants hold title or treaty land under that country's law, and it remains the country's land in international law.

rules.cite: Articles with Captain Cudjoe, Jamaica, 1739, Art. 3
rules.says: Cudjoe's people and their descendants hold about 1,500 acres near Trelawny Town for themselves and posterity forever.
Cudjoe and his successors may punish crimes among their own people, except by death. A capital case goes before a Justice of the Peace.

rules.cite: Articles with Captain Cudjoe, 1739, Art. 9 and 14
rules.says: Runaways who reach them must be returned for a reward, and white men named by the governor live with Cudjoe.
Runaways from the British colonies get asylum in Florida if they convert to Catholicism and serve four years in the militia. As reported in the history of Fort Mose.

rules.cite: Constitution of Brazil, transitional provisions (ADCT), Art. 68
rules.says: Remaining quilombo communities occupying their lands are recognised as definitive owners, and the state must issue titles.

rules.cite: Saramaka People v. Suriname, Inter-American Court of Human Rights, 2007
rules.says: Suriname must grant the Saramaka collective title under customary law, consult or get consent for projects, and pay into a US$675,000 fund. The land stays within Suriname.

zones_new.hook: A state army with roads, aircraft and satellite images, against which distance and swamp no longer protect anyone, plus the rule that a modern treaty or court win gives land rights within the country and leaves the country's sovereignty in place.
zones_new.can_you_build: Not as a new venture: this route was made by people fleeing slavery on frontiers that sources describe as inaccessible, and those forests have largely been cleared. Today's communities hold land by treaty, constitution or court ruling from the state they live in.
facts: Seven of ten major quilombos in colonial Brazil were destroyed within two years of forming (Wikipedia, Quilombo).
Descendants of Maroons are about 15% of Suriname's population and 22% of French Guiana's (Wikipedia, Maroons).
Brazil's 2022 census counted about 1.3 million quilombolas, 167,202 of them in officially delimited territories (IBGE).
In July 2023 Comissao Pro-Indio counted 211 titled quilombola territories, 62 only in part, with 1,787 titling cases pending.
The Jamaican 1739 treaty paid a reward for each runaway returned: ten shillings under the Act that accompanied it, two dollars in other accounts.
zones_new.essay:
Maroons were people in the Americas and the Indian Ocean who escaped slavery and lived in independent settlements. The word probably comes from the Spanish cimarron. They appeared early: Hispaniola's governor complained of escapees in 1503, and by the 1540s runaways controlled the island's interior, by one 1542 estimate 2,000 to 3,000 people.

Wikipedia's survey says these communities had to be inaccessible and located in inhospitable environments to last. Examples are swamps in the southern United States, canyons with sinkholes in Jamaica, and the deep jungles of the Guianas. Palmares in Brazil, the largest, stood in mountains beyond the coastal settlements for most of the 17th century, withstanding about one Portuguese expedition a year from 1672 until it fell in 1694. Most did far worse: seven of ten major Brazilian quilombos were destroyed within two years.

The ones that survived mostly did so through a deal with the colony, and the deal had a price. Jamaica's 1739 treaty gave land and internal authority, but Maroons had to hand back runaways for a reward and accept resident white officers, and later white superintendents held practical power. Yanga in New Spain, the Bahoruco leader Santiago in 1785, and San Basilio de Palenque in Colombia all accepted some version of that same condition. Castillo in Colombia refused in 1732 and was defeated in 1745. So the price of being left alone was often helping to keep slavery going, which caused tension with those still enslaved.

Treaties did not always outlast the state that signed them. Jamaica's Trelawny Town was deported overseas after a war in 1796. Wikipedia reports that independent Suriname abrogated the old Maroon treaties, and that a dam in the 1960s flooded about half of Saramaka land. The same survey says Maroon communities began to disappear in the 19th and 20th centuries as forests were razed.

The current form of this route is a land title. Brazil's 1988 Constitution recognises quilombo ownership, with the first title granted in 1995. In 2007 the Inter-American Court ordered Suriname to give the Saramaka collective title, and Cultural Survival reported in 2012 that none of the orders had been carried out. Accompong in Jamaica keeps an elected chief, and Wikipedia reports that its autonomy was ratified in 1962. All of these remain inside a state. None of the sources describes a new community forming this way today, because the conditions they name, unmapped forest and a colonial state with few soldiers, are gone in the places they cover.

sources.t: Jamaica 1739 treaty, full transcript, Slavery and Freedom Laws, UNB
Cultural Survival: Saramaka People v Suriname, a human rights victory and its messy aftermath
Politize: titling of quilombola lands in Brazil
Comissao Pro-Indio: Quilombola communities in Brazil

odds.why: These are estimates from the record. Building a hidden settlement depended on land out of a state's reach, and most Brazilian examples fell within two years. Law is low because modern protection comes through a state's own title or a human rights ruling, as with Article 68 and Saramaka. Money was farming and trade with outsiders. Holding happened mainly by treaty, as in Jamaica and Suriname, and treaties were later broken or abrogated. Recognition by other states is almost unknown, since colonies signed the deals and not foreign governments.

own.own_why: A new group gets nothing from this route, since it rested on escape from slavery into land no state could reach, and that forest has been cut or mapped. A people already on treaty or titled land does better, as in Accompong or Saramaka territory, but the state's law and courts stay above them, so few would pass the third test.

zones_new.name: Settler republics and colonisation societies
zones_new.who_owns: Every land in this group is now part of an existing country. At the time, most of it already belonged to Indigenous peoples, or was claimed by a state that had little presence there.

rules.says: Britain guarantees emigrant farmers north of the Vaal the right to govern themselves under their own laws without British interference. No slavery may be practised there.

rules.cite: US Constitution, Art. IV, Sec. 3, Cl. 1
rules.says: Congress may admit new states, but none may be formed within another state's jurisdiction without the consent of that state's legislature and of Congress.
A state should have a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and capacity to deal with other states.
A state's political existence does not depend on recognition by others, and it may organise itself and define its courts, limited only by other states' rights.

zones_new.hook: Arrival of the state whose frontier it was. Britain took Natalia and Stellaland, Germany absorbed Upingtonia, Paraguay dissolved New Australia's cooperative, and larger neighbours took most of the rest. Today nearly all dry land is already claimed, so there is no gap to move into.
zones_new.can_you_build: You can still move as a group and buy land, as Nueva Germania and New Australia did, and that leaves you under the host's law. The further step, a state of your own, worked only where land sat beyond any government's effective control, and that gap has closed.
facts: Vermont stayed outside all states for 14 years, from 1777 to 1791, and its constitution and laws continued in effect when it joined the US.
Upingtonia's land cost 300 pounds, paid as 25 firearms, a salted horse and a cask of brandy.
